author: high
claim:
Let (G=(X\sqcup Y,E)) be a finite bipartite graph. For (S\subseteq X), let

\[
N(S)=\{y\in Y: \text{(y) is adjacent to at least one vertex of (S)}\}.
\]

Prove that (G) has a matching saturating every vertex of (X) if and only if

\[
|N(S)|\ge |S|
\]

for every subset (S\subseteq X).
evidence:
A matching is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint, and it saturates X when every vertex of X is incident with one of its edges.

First suppose that G has a matching M saturating X. Fix S subseteq X. For each x in S, let m(x) be the endpoint in Y of the edge of M incident with x. Then m(x) belongs to N(S). Moreover, if x and x' are distinct, then m(x) and m(x') are distinct, since two edges of a matching cannot share a Y-endpoint. Thus m is an injection from S into N(S), and consequently |N(S)| >= |S|.

Conversely, suppose that |N(S)| >= |S| for every S subseteq X. We prove that G has a matching saturating X by induction on n=|X|.

If n=0, the empty matching saturates X. Assume n>0 and that the assertion has been proved for every finite bipartite graph whose left part has fewer than n vertices.

There are two cases.

Case 1: There is a nonempty proper subset A of X such that |N(A)|=|A|. Let H be the bipartite graph induced by the left part A and the right part N(A). For every U subseteq A, all neighbors in G of vertices of U lie in N(A), so the neighborhood of U in H is exactly N(U). Hence |N_H(U)|=|N(U)| >= |U|. Since 0<|A|<n, the induction hypothesis gives a matching M_1 in H saturating A.

Now let K be the bipartite graph induced by the left part X\A and the right part Y\N(A). We verify Hall's inequality for K. Fix T subseteq X\A. Its neighborhood in K is
N_K(T)=N(T)\N(A).
Because A and T are disjoint and N(A union T)=N(A) union N(T), the assumed inequality applied to A union T gives
|A|+|T| = |A union T| <= |N(A union T)|
= |N(A)| + |N(T)\N(A)|
= |A| + |N_K(T)|.
Cancelling |A| yields |N_K(T)| >= |T|. The left part X\A of K has fewer than n vertices, so the induction hypothesis gives a matching M_2 in K saturating X\A. The matchings M_1 and M_2 use disjoint left parts and disjoint right parts, because M_1 lies in A together with N(A), while M_2 lies in (X\A) together with (Y\N(A)). Therefore M_1 union M_2 is a matching in G saturating all of X.

Case 2: No nonempty proper subset A of X satisfies |N(A)|=|A|. Choose x in X. Applying the assumed inequality to {x} shows that N({x}) is nonempty, so choose y in N({x}). Let G' be obtained from G by deleting x and y, with left part X'=X\{x} and right part Y'=Y\{y}. We claim that G' satisfies Hall's inequality. It is immediate for the empty subset of X'. If T is a nonempty subset of X', then T is a nonempty proper subset of X. By the assumption of Case 2 and the original Hall inequality, the integers |N(T)| and |T| satisfy |N(T)| >= |T|+1. Deleting y removes at most one vertex from the neighborhood of T, and thus
|N_{G'}(T)| >= |N(T)|-1 >= |T|.
Therefore G' satisfies Hall's inequality. Its left part has n-1 vertices, so the induction hypothesis supplies a matching M' in G' saturating X'. Since neither x nor y is incident with an edge of M', adjoining the edge xy gives a matching M' union {xy} in G saturating X.

In both cases a matching saturating X exists. This proves the converse and hence the equivalence.

glossary.N(S): the neighborhood in Y of a subset S of X
glossary.M: a matching saturating X in the necessity direction
glossary.m(x): the Y-endpoint matched to x by M
glossary.A: a nonempty proper tight subset of X in Case 1
glossary.H: the subgraph induced by A and N(A)
glossary.K: the subgraph induced by X minus A and Y minus N(A)
glossary.T: an arbitrary subset of the relevant residual left part
glossary.M_1: a matching in H saturating A
glossary.M_2: a matching in K saturating X minus A
glossary.x: a chosen vertex of X in Case 2
glossary.G': the graph obtained by deleting x and y
glossary.M': a matching in G' saturating X'
